title: Expand Neurons, Not Parameters
one_liner: Splitting neurons into finer sub-neurons reduces confusion between different features without adding any extra parameters.
lead: Neural networks pack many different features into the same neuron, like a filing cabinet where each drawer holds multiple unrelated documents. This mixing causes interference: the network struggles to learn and update one feature without accidentally disturbing another. This paper shows that splitting each neuron into finer sub-neurons — like dividing one drawer into compartments — lets features breathe separately because each feature now gets its own dedicated space, so training updates to one do not ripple into others. The trick: you split without adding more weights (the stored numbers), so modern hardware still runs it fast.

problem.h2: Networks pack too many features in one neuron
paras: A neuron is a single number computed from the input. Networks use many neurons to capture many different facts about the input. But neurons often get overloaded: the same neuron encodes multiple unrelated features at once — like a single wire carrying red and blue light at the same time. This is called polysemanticity.

A beginner might try adding more neurons to separate the features. More neurons mean more weights (the stored numbers), and more weights mean the network is bigger, slower, and uses more memory — a costly tradeoff. The method in this paper finds a way to get the benefits of separation without paying that cost.

callout.html: Neurons that handle multiple features at once interfere with each other, but adding neurons costs extra weights.

steps.text: Identify neurons encoding multiple features at once.
Split weights into K smaller parts without changing the total count.
Each feature activates its own slice, not the whole neuron.
Learn which slice each feature belongs to while updating weights.
Verify that features interfere less because separate slots block collisions, and the network learns faster because learning signals are no longer mixed.

paras: The paper takes the weights inside each neuron and splits them into finer compartments. A neuron that was a single entity becomes a small collection of sub-units, each handling one feature. No new weights are added — the same budget is just arranged differently, like dividing a savings account into labeled sub-accounts without depositing more money.

hidden.name: interference between features
paras: Interference is the amount of damage one feature causes to another when they share the same neuron. If you update the weights to make one feature activate correctly, how much does that accidentally change the other feature's activation? High interference means the two features fight over the same neuron; low interference means they barely affect each other.

The paper estimates this by measuring how much accuracy drops when a feature gets displaced during training. It also uses polysemanticity metrics (measures of how many different features one neuron is encoding). When you split neurons into compartments, features collide less often, so this interference score drops.

heat.caption: Darker means more features packed into one neuron (higher interference).

reads.html: Two features in the same neuron often pull in opposite directions during training. Splitting the neuron gives each its own space to move, eliminating the tug-of-war.
Polysemanticity and feature interference are measured via loss increase when features are selectively ablated (removed). Splitting reduces this loss penalty, proving that features now interfere less.

paras: Here is the chain of cause and effect. A neuron that encodes multiple features is like a single pipe carrying multiple fluids at once. When training tries to adjust the neuron to strengthen one fluid's signal, it inevitably changes the pressure on the other fluids. This is interference.

Splitting the neuron is like replacing one pipe with three separate pipes, one per fluid. Now when training increases the pressure on one fluid (adjusts one sub-neuron's weights), the other fluids (the other sub-neurons) are not affected. Each feature gets its own dedicated pathway, so updates to one do not ripple into others. The network can now learn each feature independently without cross-talk, and training converges faster because the learning signals (the amounts by which each weight moves) are not mixed.

The paper shows this works even with random splits — the exact assignment of features to compartments matters far less than simply having separate compartments. This proves that reduced collisions, not precise matching, is the real mechanism. Modern hardware loves this because it does not care how many neurons you have; it only cares how many non-zero parameters (weights with non-zero value) you store. By keeping parameter count the same and only rearranging where those weights sit, the method plays to hardware strengths.

stages.s: raw features: red signal, blue signal, green signal
packed neuron: all three signals mixed in one wire
split into three sub-neurons: red wire, blue wire, green wire
each wire trained independently without cross-talk
cleaner signals (less noise because features are unmixed), faster learning (no cross-talk to untangle), no interference

math.words: parameter_budget is divided into K sub-neurons per neuron, each with weight sub_j. The activation of sub_j is computed the same way as before, but only uses the slice of weights allocated to it. Total parameter count stays constant.
symbols: the final activation from this neuron

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose one neuron originally has 10 parameters and encodes 3 features.
Original interference loss: feature_red moves, feature_blue drops 8 points, feature_green drops 5 points. Total damage: 13.
After splitting into 3 sub-neurons, same 10 parameters total: feature_red gets sub-neuron-1 (3 params), feature_blue gets sub-neuron-2 (4 params), feature_green gets sub-neuron-3 (3 params).
Now when feature_red moves, feature_blue and feature_green are in separate compartments. Interference loss: 0 (blue in its own slot, green in its own slot).
Same parameter budget, but interference dropped from 13 to 0.

math.note: Splitting the weight budget into independent compartments means each feature updates its own slice, with zero cross-talk from the others.

items.b: Too many compartments starves the features.
items.html: If you split one neuron into so many sub-neurons that each gets too few parameters, each sub-neuron becomes too weak to represent its feature at all. The benefit disappears.

items.b: Assigning features to the wrong compartment.
items.html: If you assign a feature to the wrong sub-neuron deliberately, you block it from learning. However, the paper shows random assignment still helps because the benefit comes from having separate compartments at all, not from perfect alignment of features to slots.
Splitting changes how data moves through the model. If your hardware cannot route sub-neuron activations efficiently, you lose the speedup from reducing interference, defeating the point.

items.b: Done right: match split width to the feature load.
items.html: If the features and compartments are balanced in number and resource demand, training runs fast and accuracy climbs across all features.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy Boolean network with 4 features encoded in 1 neuron (the packed case). Measure accuracy on each feature and the total interference score. Then split the 1 neuron into 4 sub-neurons, each with 1 feature. Measure again. Plot accuracy per feature before and after. The after plot should show all features climbing, and interference dropping to near zero, on the exact same parameter budget.
demo.metric_eq: interference_reduction = (initial_interference - final_interference) / initial_interference. accuracy_gain = average_after_accuracy - average_before_accuracy
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss that the same weight budget can separate tangled features if you split the neuron compartments.
